arguments.interpretation:
Coverage check: the dataset spans 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both October 2011 [2011-10-01,2011-11-01) and November 2011 [2011-11-01,2011-12-01) are fully contained; no partial-period truncation affects either month. Policy is retail-gbp-v1 (GBP), grain is invoice line, and net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price (unit_price > 0, cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity excluded, duplicate source lines preserved) — it is not cash collected.

Descriptive result: net_sales rose from October to November 2011 on a calendar_month basis (see evidence for exact figures). The country breakdown shows the increase is concentrated in the United Kingdom, whose positive contribution exceeds the total change; the remainder of the top five is mixed, with Netherlands and Australia contributing negatively and EIRE and Japan contributing positively. The 24-country remainder group is roughly flat and slightly negative. Because the UK contribution alone exceeds the aggregate delta, other countries collectively offset part of the UK increase — the movement is not broad-based across countries.

Interpretation is descriptive only. The catalog caveat notes that bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is not causal. No causal claim is made here; the observed pattern is consistent with a UK-driven shift but the data alone cannot establish why.
hypotheses: The November increase may be driven by a small number of large UK invoices or wholesale orders rather than a broad customer-base expansion; this would need order-level and customer-level checks to test.
Seasonal pre-holiday ordering in the UK could explain the November uplift, but no seasonal baseline from prior years is available in this dataset to confirm it.
The negative contributions from Netherlands and Australia may reflect timing of bulk orders shifting between months rather than a genuine decline in demand.
Return or cancellation adjustments concentrated in specific countries could be dampening the aggregate change; returns and gross_sales comparisons would be needed to separate this.

details.interpretation:
Coverage check: the dataset spans 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both October 2011 [2011-10-01,2011-11-01) and November 2011 [2011-11-01,2011-12-01) are fully contained; no partial-period truncation affects either month. Policy is retail-gbp-v1 (GBP), grain is invoice line, and net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price (unit_price > 0, cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity excluded, duplicate source lines preserved) — it is not cash collected.

Descriptive result: net_sales rose from October to November 2011 on a calendar_month basis (see evidence for exact figures). The country breakdown shows the increase is concentrated in the United Kingdom, whose positive contribution exceeds the total change; the remainder of the top five is mixed, with Netherlands and Australia contributing negatively and EIRE and Japan contributing positively. The 24-country remainder group is roughly flat and slightly negative. Because the UK contribution alone exceeds the aggregate delta, other countries collectively offset part of the UK increase — the movement is not broad-based across countries.

Interpretation is descriptive only. The catalog caveat notes that bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is not causal. No causal claim is made here; the observed pattern is consistent with a UK-driven shift but the data alone cannot establish why.
hypotheses: The November increase may be driven by a small number of large UK invoices or wholesale orders rather than a broad customer-base expansion; this would need order-level and customer-level checks to test.
Seasonal pre-holiday ordering in the UK could explain the November uplift, but no seasonal baseline from prior years is available in this dataset to confirm it.
The negative contributions from Netherlands and Australia may reflect timing of bulk orders shifting between months rather than a genuine decline in demand.
Return or cancellation adjustments concentrated in specific countries could be dampening the aggregate change; returns and gross_sales comparisons would be needed to separate this.
